title: Single life
hookLine: a single person has a full place in the sangat
tomorrow: Bebe twisted her ankle in the garden. who takes care of her now?

lines: AUNTY AFTER AUNTY: WHEN IS YOUR TURN?
WHY DOES THE GURU WRITE AS A BRIDE?
cards: At Jasleen's wedding, Bhua Kiran, Simran's dad's sister, got asked the same question by aunty after aunty: so, when is your turn? She laughed every time, passed the sweets, and danced at the bhangra.
Simran watched her face, and didn't laugh. Now Bhua Kiran is the one asking at the dinner table, half joking: where exactly do I fit? And Simran is stuck on something odd she noticed at the wedding.
The Lavan, the four wedding hymns, are by Guru Ram Das. So why does the Guru write as the bride? And why do the Gurus keep calling themselves the soul-bride, all through the Guru Granth Sahib?

teach.b: Here's the answer, and it's the part to tell a friend. In Gurbani, the bride isn't a woman on her wedding day.

teach.h: THE LAVAN: A SOUL WALKING TO GOD.
teach.b: The bride is the soul, every soul, and the Beloved is the Divine. When the Gurus write as brides, they write as anyone who longs for the One.
That's why the Lavan, on ang 773 and 774, can be sung at a wedding and still be about something bigger: the rounds walk a soul, step by step, toward union with God.
Two people walk them together, but the journey in the words belongs to each of them. So follow the puzzle to its end.

teach.h: THE SINGLE ONE IS IN THE STORY.
teach.b: If the deepest union in Sikh thought is the soul with the One, then a single person isn't waiting outside the main story. She's already in it.
To be honest about it, Sikh teaching honors married, householder life, and the aunties aren't wrong to love a wedding.

teach.h: A FULL PLACE, NOT HANDED OUT.
teach.b: But a full place in the sangat was never handed out at the wedding. Bhua Kiran does langar seva every week, sings the hymns by heart, and is the first one at the hospital when anyone's sick.
That's not someone in a waiting room. Simran texts her that night: you're not waiting in line. You're already the bride in every hymn.

how: Single Sikhs take part in every part of gurdwara life, from langar seva to kirtan, and the bridal imagery of Gurbani is read as describing every soul's longing for God.

o: a vow never to marry, kept by some Sikh teachers
a waiting time before a person's real life begins
a whole life, with a full place in the sangat

games.q: the bride is every soul — tap the pairs.
p: every soul, longing for the One
wrote the Lavan, as the bride

s: in the Guru Granth Sahib, the bride stands for married women
the soul-bride is every soul, which is why the Gurus write as brides.

games.q: at a family party, an uncle asks your single cousin, loudly, when she'll finally settle down. she laughs it off. what fits today's idea?
o: ask her about her own life and work, and give her the full seat.
join in kindly; everyone's only hoping she'll be happy.
change the subject to someone else's wedding plans instead.
games.why: in Gurbani the soul-bride is every soul, so a single person isn't waiting outside the story. Simran texted Bhua Kiran: you're already in it.

practice: Think of someone single in your life who gets the wedding question a lot: a cousin, a friend, an aunt.
In your head, write them a short text that has nothing to do with marriage, what you admire in them or a plan you'd like to make together, and keep their face in mind as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Single life. A whole life, with a full place in the sangat, the soul already the bride in every hymn.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Lavan, the four rounds of the Sikh wedding, by Guru Ram Das, on ang 773 and 774.

carryVoice: A full place: married or single, nobody waits in the hallway of the sangat. That's today.
